<x_0.3369><y_0.0031>C A B<x_0.5254><y_0.0227><class_Title>

<x_0.0078><y_0.0266>CABINET, or CABBINET, the molt retired place in
the fineft part of a building, fet apart for writing, flu-
dying, or preferving any thing that is precious.<x_0.8076><y_0.0734><class_Text>

<x_0.04><y_0.0719>A complete apartment conflits of a hall, anti-cham-
ber, chamber, and cabinet, with a gallery on one fide.
Hence we fay, a cabinet of paintings, curiolities, _Gc_.<x_0.8066><y_0.1164><class_Text>

<x_0.0137><y_0.1156>CABINET alfo denotes a piece of joiner's workmanhip,
being a kind of prefs or chef), with feveral doors and
drawers.<x_0.8057><y_0.1586><class_Text>

<x_0.041><y_0.1594>There are common cabinets of oak or of chefnut,
varnified cabinets of China and Japan, cabinets or in-
laid work, and fome of ebony, or the like ficarce and
precious woods.<x_0.8047><y_0.218><class_Text>

<x_0.042><y_0.2172>Formerly the Dutch and German cabinets were
much effeemed in France, but are now quite out of
date, as well as the cabinets of ebony, which came
from Venice.<x_0.8086><y_0.275><class_Text>

<x_0.0166><y_0.2742>CABIRI, a term in the theology of the ancient Pagans,
figifying great and powerful gods; being a name
given to the gods of Samothracia. They were alfo
workhipped in other parts of Greece, as Lemnos and
Thebes, where the cabiria were celebrated in honour
of them: thefe gods are laid to be, in number,
four, _viz._ Axieros, Axiocerfa, Axiocerfus, and
Cafmilus.<x_0.8096><y_0.3922><class_Text>

<x_0.0176><y_0.3914>CABIRIA, feffivals in honour of the cabiri, celebrated
in Thebes and Lemnos, but especially in Samothra-
cia, an illand confecrated to the cabiri. All who were
initiated into the myfferies of thefe gods, were thought
to be feured thereby from florms at fea, and all other
dangers. The ceremony of initiation was performed
by placing the candidate, crowned with olive-branches,
and girded about the loins with a purple ribband, on
a kind of throne, about which the prieils, and perfons
before initiated, danced.<x_0.8105><y_0.5375><class_Text>

<x_0.0186><y_0.5367>CABLAN, the nam: of a kingdom and city of India,
beyond the Ganges.<x_0.8115><y_0.5672><class_Text>

<x_0.0195><y_0.5656>CABLE, a thick, large, frong rope, commonly of
hemp, which ferves to keep a hip at anchor.<x_0.8125><y_0.5969><class_Text>

<x_0.0527><y_0.5961>There is no merchant-hip, however weak, but has
at leaft three cables ; namely, the chief cable, or
cable of the fleet-anchor, a common cable, and a
fmaller one.<x_0.8037><y_0.6539><class_Text>

<x_0.0547><y_0.6531>Cable is alfo faid of ropes, which ferve to raife
heavy loads, by the help of cranes, pullies, and other
engines. The name of cable is ufually given to fuch
as have, at leaft, three inches in diameter ; thofe that
are lefs are only called ropes of different names, ac-
cording to their ufe.<x_0.8135><y_0.7422><class_Text>

<x_0.0566><y_0.7398>Every cable, of what thickness foever it be, is com-
pofed of three friends ; every frand of three ropes ; and
every rope of three twifts : the twift is made of more
or lefs threads, according as the cable is to be thicker
or thinner.<x_0.8145><y_0.8133><class_Text>

<x_0.0576><y_0.8141>In the manufacture of cables, after the ropes are
made, they ufe flicks, which they pafs frit between
the ropes of which they make the frants, and after-
wards between the frants of which they make the
cable, to the end that they may all twift the better;
and be more regularly wound together ; and alfo, to
prevent them from twining or intangling, they hang,<x_0.8174><y_0.918><class_Text>
